question.text: Nakshatra Cat III Long-Short AIF identifies a Post-Earnings-Announcement-Drift (PEAD) pattern in Indian mid-caps. The strategy loads up on positive earnings surprises for 30 trading days post-announcement. Which best characterises this opportunity from an EMH standpoint?

answer.text: PEAD is a well-documented anomaly inconsistent with semi-strong efficiency (prices under-react to public earnings news); the strategy can generate alpha, BUT limits to arbitrage - costs, capacity, liquidity and crowding - may erode the edge over time.
PEAD is consistent with strong-form efficiency, so the strategy is doomed.
PEAD violates SEBI rules and cannot be executed by a Cat III AIF.
PEAD is purely a random-walk phenomenon with no exploitable structure.

explanation.text: The Logic: PEAD is a classic semi-strong-form anomaly (prices do NOT instantly/fully reflect earnings surprises) and sits in the broader under-reaction/momentum family. Cat III hedge funds can exploit it, but limits to arbitrage (transaction costs, impact cost, capacity, borrow availability for shorts, strategy crowding) can shrink alpha - consistent with the 'internal contradiction' argument. The Trap: Option B inverts - strong form would NEGATE any such alpha. Option C invents a non-existent SEBI ban. Option D contradicts the anomaly literature. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM), XV (RA), VIII (Equity Derivatives) frame PEAD and momentum at portfolio level. XIX-C angle: as a Cat III manager you must document strategy capacity and anticipated alpha decay in the PPM. Manager's Pro-Tip: Size your PEAD strategy against daily turnover and short-borrow availability - publish an honest 'alpha decay' expectation in quarterly letters. LPs respect front-running of your own capacity limits over surprise strategy shutdowns.
